resumen: What each format keeps and which one to pick depending on whether you will edit or share.

bloques.alt: Two files of the same photo. On the left, the JPEG: a small file, already processed by the camera and ready to share, with little room to edit: 1, JPEG. On the right, the RAW: a much bigger file, with almost all the sensor's data and lots of room to edit, but it has to be developed before sharing: 2, RAW.
bloques.pie: 1 JPEG: small and ready, with little room to edit. 2 RAW: big, for editing, with lots of room.

bloques.texto: A JPEG is the photo already developed by the camera; a RAW is the digital negative: it weighs more, but leaves much more room to edit.

A [[jpeg|JPEG]] is the photo already processed by the camera and compressed: it takes little space and you can share it directly, but compression throws away some of the data. A [[raw|RAW]] keeps almost everything the sensor captured, unprocessed: it takes much more space and you have to develop it with editing software. Unedited, a RAW looks flat, and a JPEG looks livelier.

items: More room to edit: you can change the white balance and the exposure, and recover highlights and shadows with less noise.
A JPEG takes big changes worse: banding and odd colors show up.
It works better with difficult light and for fixing mistakes, and gives more quality in big prints.
Small files: more photos fit on the card and they move faster.
Ready to share, with no editing.
Longer bursts: the camera stores more JPEGs in a row than RAWs before it slows down.

bloques.texto: If you are going to edit, or the light is difficult, shoot RAW. If you want to share right away, or you are short on space, shoot JPEG. With RAW+JPEG the camera saves both versions of each photo, a JPEG to share and a RAW to edit later, at the cost of filling the card sooner. If in doubt, start with that.

On many phones you can shoot RAW: on some it is turned on in the camera settings or in Pro mode, and on others you need a separate app. The files weigh much more. And a phone's JPEG is already so worked on that, unedited, it often looks good.
If your camera allows it, set RAW+JPEG and take a photo with lots of contrast. Open both in an editor and lift the shadows on each. Compare.
